# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from Slack to Element, particularly due to concerns about data ownership and cost. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce expenses.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Element allows users to retain full ownership of their data, whereas Slack's terms and conditions apply to user data.
* Setup complexity: Slack has a more straightforward setup process, while Element requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are scalable, but Element's self-hosted nature allows for more customization and control.
* Feature difference: Element has end-to-end encryption for all conversations, whereas Slack only offers this feature for certain paid plans.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with other tools
* Good mobile app support
* Robust customer support
* Limited control over data ownership
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* End-to-end encryption for all conversations
* Customizable and scalable
* Retain full ownership of data
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a better choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and don't mind paying for a proprietary service. It's ideal for small to medium-sized teams that need a straightforward communication platform with a wide range of integrations. On the other hand, Element is suitable for teams that value data ownership and customization. It's perfect for larger teams or organizations that require a high level of control over their communication platform and are willing to invest time in setting it up.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack export tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's conversations and other data.
2. Set up an Element server and create a new account.
3. Use the Element import tool to import your Slack data from the JSON file.
4. Configure your Element server and customize it according to your team's needs.
5. Invite your team members to join the new Element server and start using it.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its self-hosting requirements and limited customer support. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Element's scalability can be affected by the server's hardware and configuration. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, Element is a great alternative to Slack, and we recommend switching to Element if you have a large team and are willing to invest time in setting it up.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) that require a high level of control over their communication platform and don't need phone support.
* Organizations that handle sensitive information and require end-to-end encryption for all conversations.
* Teams that are already self-hosting other services and have the technical expertise to set up and maintain an Element server.
* Businesses that prioritize data ownership and are willing to invest time in setting up a customized communication platform.
* Developers who need a customizable and scalable communication platform for their projects.

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, which means you can use it without paying any subscription fees. However, you'll need to cover the costs of hosting your own server.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element has a steeper learning curve due to its self-hosting requirements and customization options. However, it provides more control over your data and communication platform.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data using the Slack export tool and import it into Element using the Element import tool.
### Does Element have phone support?
No, Element does not offer phone support, but it has a community-driven support system and extensive documentation.
### Is Element suitable for small teams?
Not necessarily, as Element's self-hosting requirements and customization options may be overwhelming for small teams. However, small teams that value data ownership and customization may still find Element suitable.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack has a more straightforward setup process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, while Slack requires a third-party integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Strong mobile app support
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data storage and security
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Customizable and extensible through plugins
* Strong support for developer teams
* Free, open-source option
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
### Slack
Slack is a good choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's well-suited for small to medium-sized teams that need a simple, intuitive communication platform. Teams with complex integration requirements may also prefer Slack due to its wide range of third-party integrations.
### Mattermost
Mattermost is a good choice for teams that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setting up and maintaining their own server. It's well-suited for large teams or enterprises with strict security and compliance requirements. Developer teams may also prefer Mattermost due to its customizable and extensible nature.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to import your Slack data, which supports JSON format.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance to match your team's requirements, including setting up plugins and integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure a smooth transition for your team.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for many users, offering a high degree of customizability and control over data. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's self-hosted option requires significant technical expertise to set up and maintain. For teams that don't require full control over their data and prioritize ease of use, Slack may still be the better choice. However, for teams that value data ownership and are willing to invest time in setup and maintenance, Mattermost is a clear winner.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need complex integrations and want to save on costs.
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that require full control over their data and are willing to invest time in setup and maintenance.
* Large teams (50-200 users) that need to reduce costs and are comfortable with self-hosting.
* Developer teams that require customizable and extensible communication platforms.
* Teams with strict security and compliance requirements that need full control over their data.

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option that allows teams to host their own servers and have full control over their data.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost has a free, open-source option, but self-hosting requires server costs.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with third-party apps?
Yes, Mattermost has a wide range of integrations with third-party apps, including GitHub and Jira.
### Is Slack more secure than Mattermost?
Both Slack and Mattermost have robust security features, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more control over data storage and security.

# Discord vs Element

## Overview

Chat platform popular with gaming and developer communities. is a popular proprietary tool in the communication space. Element is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Discord costs Free / $9.99/month; Element is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Discord is Proprietary; Element is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Element can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Element eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Element has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Discord

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Element

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [element-hq/element-web](https://github.com/element-hq/element-web) * ~11k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Discord if:** Discord is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Element if:** Element is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Discord in its standard export format, review Element import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Element is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Discord tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Element instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Discord, switching to self-hosted Element will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Discord until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Discord paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Element free to use?
Yes. Element is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Discord to Element?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Discord data, follow the Element import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Element get regular updates?
Yes. Element has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Element without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Element development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced May 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Discord](https://discord.com) and [Element](https://element.io) before making decisions.*

# GitHub vs GitLab (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and GitLab are two popular version control systems used for software development, offering a range of tools for collaborative coding, project management, and deployment. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to choose between the two platforms or considering switching from one to the other, particularly for those seeking more control over their data or customizability. The core use case for both tools is version control and collaborative software development.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free and paid plans, while GitLab offers a free self-hosted option and a paid SaaS option.
* Data ownership: GitLab allows for self-hosting, giving users full control over their data, whereas GitHub stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub is generally easier to set up, while GitLab requires more technical expertise, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Both platforms are highly scalable, but GitLab's self-hosted option provides more flexibility for large enterprises.
* Feature difference: GitLab offers built-in CI/CD pipelines, while GitHub relies on third-party integrations for similar functionality.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### GitHub
* Easy to set up and use
* Large community and ecosystem
* Integrates well with other GitHub tools
* Offers free and paid plans
* Limited control over data for free plan
### GitLab
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* Built-in CI/CD pipelines
* Highly customizable
* Free self-hosted option
* Steeper learning curve
* Limited support for some third-party integrations

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who prioritize ease of use and a large community of users. It's ideal for those who don't require full control over their data or customizability. On the other hand, GitLab is a better choice for large enterprises or organizations that require self-hosting, customizability, and full control over their data. It's also suitable for teams that need built-in CI/CD pipelines and are willing to invest time in setting up and configuring the platform.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Set up a new GitLab instance, either self-hosted or SaaS.
3. Use the GitLab Import/Export tool to import your GitHub repository.
4. Configure any necessary settings, such as CI/CD pipelines and permissions.
5. Test your migrated repository to ensure everything is working correctly.

## Our Take
GitLab is a production-ready platform for most users, offering a wide range of features and customizability. However, it's essential to note that GitLab's self-hosting option can be complex to set up and requires significant technical expertise. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that GitLab's built-in CI/CD pipelines can be resource-intensive and may require additional hardware or configuration to run efficiently. We recommend switching to GitLab for teams that require self-hosting, customizability, and full control over their data, while GitHub remains a better choice for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who prioritize ease of use.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that require self-hosting and customizability
* Medium-sized teams (10-50 users) that need built-in CI/CD pipelines and are willing to invest time in setup and configuration
* Large enterprises (over 100 users) that require full control over their data and customizability
* Teams that prioritize data ownership and security
* Developers who need advanced features and customizability

## FAQ
### Is GitLab free?
GitLab offers a free self-hosted option, as well as a free SaaS plan with limited features.
### Can I self-host GitHub?
No, GitHub does not offer self-hosting options.
### Is GitLab compatible with GitHub?
Yes, GitLab is compatible with GitHub, and you can import your GitHub repository using the GitLab Import/Export tool.
### Does GitLab offer CI/CD pipelines?
Yes, GitLab offers built-in CI/CD pipelines, which can be resource-intensive and require additional hardware or configuration.
### Can I use GitLab for personal projects?
Yes, GitLab is suitable for personal projects, offering a free self-hosted option and a range of features for collaborative coding and project management.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are two popular design and prototyping tools used by designers, developers, and product teams to create user interfaces, websites, and mobile applications. This comparison is beneficial for teams and individuals who are considering switching from Figma to Penpot, possibly due to the core use case of needing a free or self-hosted solution. The key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their design data.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Figma stores design data on its proprietary servers, whereas Penpot allows users to self-host and maintain full control over their data.
* Setup complexity: Figma has a more streamlined onboarding process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and complex projects, whereas Penpot is still developing its scalability features.
* Integration difference: Figma has a more extensive library of third-party plugins and integrations, while Penpot has a growing but limited set of integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface and onboarding process
	+ Extensive library of third-party plugins and integrations
	+ Scalable and suitable for large teams and complex projects
	+ Real-time collaboration features
	+ Access to a large community of designers and developers
* Cons:
	+ Expensive, especially for large teams
	+ Limited control over design data
	+ Proprietary license
### Penpot
* Pros:
	+ Completely free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full control over design data
	+ Growing community of developers and designers
	+ Customizable and extensible
	+ Suitable for small to medium-sized teams and projects
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve due to technical requirements
	+ Limited scalability features
	+ Limited library of third-party plugins and integrations
	+ Still in active development, with some features missing or incomplete

## When to Choose Each
Figma is suitable for large teams, complex projects, and organizations that require a scalable and feature-rich design solution. It is ideal for teams that need a user-friendly interface, extensive integrations, and real-time collaboration features. On the other hand, Penpot is a better choice for small to medium-sized teams, individuals, or organizations that prioritize data ownership, customizability, and cost-effectiveness. Penpot is also a good option for teams that are comfortable with self-hosting and have the technical expertise to set it up.

## Migration Path

5. Test and refine your designs in Penpot to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is still in active development, and while it shows great promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Penpot's scalability features are still limited, which may affect performance for large teams or complex projects. However, for small to medium-sized teams or individuals who prioritize data ownership and cost-effectiveness, Penpot is a viable alternative to Figma, and we recommend considering it as an option.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who do not need extensive scalability features
* Individuals or freelancers who prioritize data ownership and customizability
* Organizations with limited budgets that cannot afford Figma's expensive plans
* Teams that require self-hosting for security or compliance reasons
* Designers or developers who are comfortable with technical setup and maintenance
